article.title: Impeachment Could Become A Powerful Tool
article.author: Paul deLespinasse
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Some Democrats are threatening to impeach Donald Trump again in January when they have the majority in the House and Senate But enough Republicans will remain to block conviction since they will constitute more than one third of the Senate. Perhaps the third time would be the charm, since some Republican politicians are distancing themselves from him. But a successful impeachment probably needs to be led by Republicans. If initiated by Democrats, many Republicans would argue that the impeachment is just another partisan attack. However Democrats should not abandon all thoughts of impeachment. Rather than impeaching Donald Trump, however, they should impeach his more outrageous subordinates beginning with Pete Hegseth, Todd Blanche, Russell Vought, and Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Regrettably, Stephen Miller--- Trump’s new chief of staff--- is not considered a “civil officer” of the U.S. and therefore probably cannot be impeached. Representative Thomas Massie (R-Kentucky) may introduce a resolution to impeach Hegseth this week, and it may well pass the House even before Democrats have taken over because many Republicans can’t stand him. A president’s associates, as we will see, are more likely to be convicted by the required two-thirds Senate majority than he is. My Ph.D. dissertation examined the role of the king or queen in six constitutional monarchies. The history of Great Britain, the Netherlands, Belgium, Norway, Sweden, and Denmark indicates that removing a leader’s subordinates can be a powerful way to control what that hereditary leader is doing. Related: One Sided View of Preposterous Lawsuit At PBS The old idea that “the king can do no wrong” persists in these countries despite the fact that they are democracies. These apparently conflicting facts are reconciled by requiring that royal decisions must have the “countersignature” of a minister who can be held accountable and ousted by the parliament. These countries thereby enjoy a strict separation of two roles. The monarch is ceremonial head of state. The prime minister is head of government. The monarch is theoretically all-powerful, but actual decisions are made by the cabinet under the leadership of the prime minister. The American presidency combines the two roles--- head of state and head of government--- in a single official. But like constitutional monarchs, the president, acting individually, has little actual power. Presidential decisions will have no real consequences unless they are carried out by subordinates--- cabinet members and the other people employed by their various departments. The analogy with the European monarchies, like all analogies, is not an exact one. In the United States, cabinet members are not picked by Congress and cannot be members of Congress. But thanks to the impeachment power set forth in the Constitution, cabinet members can be removed by Congress. And the Senate can block replacements put forward by the president. Our federal Constitution has no provisions for recalling the president. To the extent that American presidents are politically immune from removal by impeachment, they are therefore much like the unelected European monarchs. But the same limitation does not apply to impeachment of that president’s advisors and staff. Related: A Major Political Question: To Whom Did God Give Land? It will be easier to convince two-thirds of the Senate to convict mere presidential advisors than to convict the president. Impeachment supporters from the president’s party can argue that their loyalty to the president is firm but that the advisor has been giving the president bad advice. It would therefore be harder for a president to threaten to “primary” senators who, professing support for him, simply vote to remove the advisor. Removing an advisor would give the president both a motive and a face-saving way to reverse policies that the removed official had been administering. Although Harry Truman’s desk sign that “the buck stops here” would remain true, the advisor could be the scapegoat for problems that really were the president’s responsibility. And critics of the policy should be happy to see it reversed, even if the ultimately guilty president remains in office. Impeaching presidential advisors could become an important part of American government despite its repeated failure to remove presidents. It would strengthen the hand of Congress, today a weakened body despite the intent of those who wrote the Constitution to make it the strongest branch of government. It is not impossible for a president’s party to turn on him, as Richard Nixon found out. But the future importance of impeachment may lie mainly in its use to remove presidential advisors and, hopefully, reverse policies with which they have been associated.
